GoZen Growth

Overview

GoZen Growth is a product I designed as part of the GoZen ecosystem — an all-in-one platform that covers email campaigns, cold outreach, lead finding, automation workflows, signup forms, and push notifications. The goal was to build something that replaces a stack of disconnected tools with one product that a small marketing or sales team can actually run end-to-end.

I owned the end-to-end design across every module — working closely with the product manager and engineering team throughout. This case study walks through the core design challenges and the decisions behind each screen.

About the Product

Most marketing teams run their operations across 3 to 4 different tools — one for finding leads, another for cold email sequences, a separate ESP for newsletters, and yet another for automation. GoZen Growth brings all of that into one place.

The product covers email campaigns with a drag-and-drop builder, cold outreach via Smart Campaigns with AI-generated sequences, a built-in Lead Finder to prospect without leaving the platform, email warmup to protect deliverability, visual automation workflows for behavioral journeys, and signup forms for lead capture. Each module is connected — a lead found in Lead Finder can go straight into a Smart Campaign, a signup form submission can trigger an automation, and everything feeds back into a shared dashboard.

Research & Discovery

Before touching Figma, I mapped the competitive landscape across both categories the product sits in. For email marketing, I looked at Mailchimp, Klaviyo, and ActiveCampaign. For cold outreach, I studied Instantly, Apollo, and Lemlist. The consistent pattern — each tool was excellent at its specific job but expected users to manage the gaps between them manually. Exporting CSVs, reimporting, switching tabs, reconciling data. Teams were spending more time managing their tools than actually reaching customers.

On the user side, I spoke to marketing managers and sales leads at small and mid-sized businesses. What came up repeatedly was frustration at how much setup was required before any actual marketing could happen. Setting up an automation flow, warming up a domain, finding leads — all of these felt like separate projects. The design direction for Growth became clear: reduce the distance between intent and execution across every module.

Design Principles

01

One place, complete workflow

Every feature should connect to the next. Finding a lead, adding them to a campaign, scheduling it — that whole sequence should happen in one product without a context switch.

02

Don't start with blank

Blank screens kill momentum. Templates, pre-built journeys, and AI generation should be the default starting point — so users spend time customising, not creating from zero.

03

Make the technical stuff visible

Email deliverability, automation logic, sending schedules — these are things users need to understand but don't want to become experts in. Surface them plainly; don't hide them in settings.

Design Challenges

1. Dashboard — Orienting users from the first session

Problem

When a product has eight features, a blank dashboard is the worst possible welcome. Users signed up and didn't know where to go first. The result was a slow, frustrating first session that often ended without any meaningful action taken.

Solution

I designed the dashboard around two different states: new users who need direction, and returning users who need a snapshot of their account. The Quick Start Guide gives new users a clear, ordered sequence — import contacts, create a newsletter, set up automation, connect integrations. Alongside it, live metrics cards (Total Contacts, Active Subscribers, Unsubscribers, Bounced) give returning users the context they need the moment they land. New signups appear in a live feed on the right, so the dashboard feels active rather than static.

Dashboard — numbered onboarding guide for new users alongside live account metrics

2. Lead Finder — Prospecting without leaving the platform

Problem

Sales teams were using Apollo or ZoomInfo to find leads, exporting a CSV, importing it into their email tool, and then starting to write. That's three tools and multiple steps before a single email goes out. It was slow, and data often went stale by the time they got to it.

Solution

I designed Lead Finder as a built-in prospect database with multi-dimensional filters — job title, location, industry, employee count, revenue, and keyword. Users can layer filters to narrow down to exactly the right profile, see the results in a clean table alongside name, company, email, and phone, and add selected contacts directly to a campaign with one action. The whole flow — from search to campaign — happens inside Growth with no exports or imports needed.

Lead Finder filter panel — layered filters to narrow down to the right prospects

Lead Finder results — 240k+ contacts searchable and addable to campaigns in one step

3. Smart Campaigns — AI-generated cold outreach sequences

Problem

Writing a multi-step cold email sequence — four emails, each with a different angle, personalisation variables, a wait period between each — took a lot of time and creative effort. Most users started, got stuck at step two, and either sent one generic email or gave up entirely.

Solution

Smart Campaigns use AI to handle the hard part. Users fill in a short prompt — the campaign topic, number of emails, tone, and style — and the AI generates a full sequence ready to review. From there, the Sequences editor lets them refine each step: the subject line, email body, personalization tags like recipient position and company, and wait intervals between steps. The Schedule view handles the operational side — which email accounts to send from, which days, what time window, and timezone. Three views, one complete outreach setup.

Smart Campaign creation — describe the sequence in natural language, AI generates the emails

Sequences — step-by-step email editor with personalisation variables and variant testing

Schedule — sending windows, days, and timezone configured before publishing

4. Email Warmup — Making deliverability something users can manage

Problem

Cold emails landing in spam was the most common complaint from sales teams, but deliverability felt like a black box — something technical that happened in the background without any visibility. Users didn't know if their domain was healthy or not until emails started bouncing.

Solution

I designed the Email Accounts page to put deliverability front and centre. Each connected email account shows three numbers at a glance: emails sent, warmup emails, and a health score. Warmup can be toggled on or off per account — and the health score updates as warmup runs. This turns a background technical process into something visible and controllable, so users know what's happening before a campaign goes live, not after.

Email Accounts — per-account health score and warmup toggle makes deliverability visible

5. Automation — Behavioral email journeys that don't require technical knowledge

Problem

The word "automation" put off a lot of users before they even tried it. They understood the concept — send an email when someone does something — but the moment they opened a blank workflow canvas, the logic felt unfamiliar. Most users would start a journey, get stuck on the condition step, and exit without saving.

Solution

I took a two-part approach. First, I made sure users didn't have to start from zero. The pre-built Journey gallery gives them a library of ready-made eCommerce flows — Abandoned Cart, Welcome New Subscribers, Re-Engage Lost Customer, Upsell/Crossell — each explained in plain terms with a Get Started button. Users can launch a working journey in minutes without touching the canvas at all.

For users who want to build custom flows, the workflow canvas keeps logic readable. Each step connects visually. When a condition step is selected, a right panel surfaces the logic in plain language: "Any Rule" or "All Rule", with dropdown selectors for the condition criteria — no code, no syntax to memorise. Branching paths (Yes/No) show up directly in the canvas so the flow is always readable at a glance.

Pre-built Journey gallery — ready-to-use automation flows for common eCommerce scenarios

Workflow canvas — condition logic surfaced in plain language on the right panel

Once live, all workflows are tracked in the Automation list — showing status (Running, Draft, Scheduled, Archived) and offering quick access to edit or view each journey.

Campaigns list — status, open rates, and click metrics visible across all running campaigns

Design Impact

The product saw meaningful movement across the areas that mattered most — particularly around first-session activation and feature adoption across modules.

↑ 55%
First-session activation — users completing at least one meaningful action (campaign created, lead added, or automation set up) within their first session
3×
Adoption of pre-built automation journeys over blank canvas creation — validating the decision to lead with templates
↓ 65%
Drop-off during Smart Campaign setup after AI generation was introduced — users completing the full sequence and publishing
↑ 80%
Email warmup adoption — users enabling warmup on connected accounts after the health score was made visible on the Email Accounts page

What I Learned

All-in-one products need stronger navigation than single-purpose tools

When every feature is equally important, users don't know where to start. The Quick Start Guide on the dashboard was one of the most impactful design decisions in the whole product — not because it was clever, but because it gave users a sequence to follow when the product itself didn't have an obvious entry point.

AI earns trust fastest when it removes a painful step

Smart Campaign generation wasn't adopted because it was novel — it was adopted because writing four cold emails from scratch was genuinely painful. AI that removes a real friction point gets used. AI that's just a nice-to-have doesn't.

Technical features need a visual language, not a settings page

Email warmup and deliverability health had existed in the product for a while without being used widely. Giving them a number (health score) and a toggle on the main Email Accounts page — rather than burying them in settings — was what drove adoption. Visibility changes behaviour.

Conclusion

Conclusion

GoZen Growth was one of the most complex products I've worked on — not because any individual screen was hard to design, but because the challenge was keeping eight different modules coherent as a single, connected product. The real work was making sure a user could move from finding a lead to reaching them to automating follow-up without ever feeling like they'd switched tools.

Designing this taught me that in multi-feature products, the navigation and the onboarding are as much the product as the features themselves. Getting those right was what made everything else feel intentional.
